claims.text: Local chemical ordering governs the onset of premelting and melting in Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles.
Copper preferentially segregates to the surfaces of Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles.
Copper surface segregation induces lattice distortions.
Localized elemental segregation creates regions of heterogeneous and reduced cohesive energy.
Copper has a lower melting point than the other components relevant to the proposed mechanism.
Reduced local cohesive energy at copper-enriched sites promotes early atomic mobility and surface premelting.
As-synthesized Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles possess chemical inhomogeneities arising from synthesis.
The as-synthesized baseline includes copper segregation.
Post-synthesis annealing reduces segregation and produces a more homogeneous elemental distribution.
Annealing-induced compositional homogenization reduces localized low-cohesion regions and delays premelting.
Particles with copper-enriched surfaces will begin premelting at lower temperatures than homogenized annealed particles.
Surface effects are significant for nanoparticles in the proposed 5–50 nm size range.
An inert atmosphere or vacuum avoids oxidation during heating.
The proposed mechanism may not extend to bulk material or alloy systems having different elemental melting points or interaction behavior.
Particle size, segregation degree, and synthesis conditions affect the magnitude of the premelting-temperature shift.
Nanoparticle morphology and interfacial energies may also influence premelting and melting behavior.
